candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe medication systems and error prevention
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize a structured, interdisciplinary medication-safety response to drug shortages.

options.A: Stop the medication for every client without assessing therapeutic alternatives.
options.B: Continue usual use until all remaining stock is exhausted.
options.C: Use a coordinated shortage plan that identifies appropriate alternatives, conserves or prioritizes supply when indicated, and clearly communicates practice changes to staff.
options.D: Inform prescribers only and allow other clinical staff to learn changes informally.

candidate.rationale: ASHP shortage-management resources emphasize organized strategies to maintain effective patient care, including therapeutic alternatives and management/conservation approaches. Drug shortages can contribute to medication errors, so changes must be managed deliberately rather than through unplanned depletion or informal communication. Therefore C is best.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Drug shortages require organized management to maintain patient care; ASHP resources include therapeutic alternatives and management/conservation strategies and identify medication-error risk from shortages.
candidate.source_document_title: Drug Shortages — Guidelines and Tools / Shortage Resources
candidate.source_locator: Shortage Resources — Managing Drug Shortages; Guidelines and Tools — ASHP Guidelines on Managing Drug Product Shortages and current management/conservation resources
candidate.stem: A hospital is managing a national shortage of a frequently used medication. Which approach best supports medication safety during the shortage?
